frontmatter.title: Adiabatic intuition and a digitized anneal
frontmatter.description: An explicit four-qubit MaxCut anneal, continuous numerical reference, separate digitization checks, and a qualified gap diagnostic.

children.value: Adiabatic optimization starts from an easily prepared low-energy state and changes the Hamiltonian toward one whose low-energy states encode solutions

. Interference arises through that evolution rather than a classical search over independent layer angles. How slowly the path must be followed depends on its spectral structure and smoothness. There is no generic polynomial runtime promise for an arbitrary optimization problem.
This example uses the same four-vertex cycle and classical MaxCut reference as
. It implements a digitized time-dependent anneal with explicit gates, not an analog-hardware experiment. The target, time, and number of slices are chosen before examining the studies.

children.value: . Increasing path time addresses the ideal evolution’s preparation quality. Refining slices addresses digitization relative to the continuous numerical reference. They are different changes with different errors, and the plots retain that distinction.
The fixed main digitized anneal uses

, chosen before the studies. The input is the four-vertex cycle and the initial state is |+> on each qubit. H_D = -sum X, H_P = 0.5 sum ZZ = 2-C, and the linear path is H(s) = (1-s) H_D + s H_P. Evolution times are Hamiltonian units with ℏ=1, rather than hardware execution times.
The main circuit’s exact ideal maximum-cut probability is
. The predeclared probability target ≥0.95 was met:

. The independent continuous DOP853 reference has maximum-cut probability 0.987036431. Circuit-versus-reference state infidelity is 1.19e-08; absolute mean-cut error is 2.74e-05. These are state-specific numerical checks, rather than operator-error or global adiabatic guarantees.

The main continuous reference uses SciPy DOP853 with rtol=1e-11, atol=1e-13, 1973 derivative evaluations, and recorded norm drift 6.1e-13. Solver tolerances are numerical settings, not certified error bounds.

The 201-point gap scan has a smallest sampled G=+1 sector gap of 1.010939045. The full gap is zero at s=1 because two cut states are degenerate. The initial state lies in the conserved G=X⊗4, G=+1 sector. A positive finite-grid sector diagnostic does not certify a gap everywhere, an adiabatic runtime theorem, or behavior on another graph.
All time/step studies and dense ODE calculations are classical simulations with
. The three main-circuit readouts below use ideal multinomial counts, not hardware executions. Their sample variance scores each complete cut jointly; estimated standard errors are descriptive.
Per main circuit: H 4, RX 2048, RZ 1024, CX 2048, measurement 4. The modeled protocol totals

. The ledger repeats every preparation, driver rotation, explicit edge interaction, and final measurement for all shots. Physical reset/measurement time, routing, rotation synthesis, fault correction and hardware runtime are excluded. Arbitrary rotations remain unsynthesized in this logical ledger. Any conditional physical projection is a separate report.

The recorded bounded CPU workflow took 2.565495 s for circuit simulation, dense references, gap diagnostics and ideal sampling. Artifact drawing, export and logical-ledger compilation are outside that timer; it is not quantum hardware time.
